newsitem.title: USA: Demand for FBI files on CIA nominee sparks dispute.
newsitem.headline: Demand for FBI files on CIA nominee sparks dispute.

text.p: A demand by the chairman of the Senate Intelligence Committee for full FBI files on CIA nominee Anthony Lake came under fire on Friday by senior members of both political parties.
Chairman Richard Shelby, an Alabama Republican, said that unless the files were made available he would not hold a hearing on the Lake nomination as scheduled on March 11.

Shelby said he was not satisfied with the FBI summaries given to the committee, likening them to "a second grade 'Weekly Reader.'" He and a group of conservative Republican senators want more extensive files to be made available not only to committee members but to all interested senators.
White House spokesman Mike McCurry called the information request "extraordinary" and said talks were under way to try to reach an accord on information to be provided.

Shelby's demand threw a new roadblock in the way of Lake's confirmation by the Senate nearly three months after President Clinton picked his national security adviser to head the Central Intelligence Agency.

In a Senate speech, Connecticut Democrat Joseph Lieberman decried increasing demands for information of Lake's involvement in administration actions and policies, saying he was being held to "an impossible and unfair" standard.
"Let's not subject this ... patriot to a kind of water torture," Lieberman said.
Committee Vice Chairman Bob Kerrey, a Nebraska Democrat, said the delays on Lake's hearing threatened to unravel the committee's traditional bipartisanship.
He disagreed that the FBI information provided was inadequate and added: "Some people are just looking for any reason at all to vote against him ... for ideological reasons."

Kerrey said Shelby had told him he wanted "all the files" without specifying exactly what he meant. Republican committee member Pat Roberts of Kansas has called for "a complete file" and "full disclosure of all information" including that gathered in earlier other background investigations.

A senior Republican on the Intelligence Committee, Sen. Richard Lugar of Indiana, said "raw" FBI files frequently contained unevaluated -- sometimes scandalous -- allegations and gossip collected by the FBI.

He said such files were sometimes made available to the chairmen and top minority members of committees considering high nominations but were not given broader circulation. Doing so in this case would be unfair to Lake, he said.

A letter sent to Senate Republican Leader Trent Lott by Sen. Phil Gramm of Texas, chairman of the conservative Republican Senate Steering Committee, and signed by 16 senators, recalled the bitter fight eight years ago over President George Bush's nomination of the late Sen. John Tower as defence secretary.
The Senate rejected the nomination following airing of charges of drinking and womanizing. Lugar noted many Republicans were still angered by the Tower battle.
Gramm's letter said Tower's complete FBI file was placed in a secure room for all senators to read and called for similar action on Lake's files.
But Kerrey told reporters that in fact Tower's files had been restricted to Armed Services Committee members and called the standard of privacy then "pitifully low."
"Let's not require an invasion of privacy far beyond what we've required anybody else to go through, including Sen. Tower," Kerrey said.
He said Roberts's request for data from previous investigations appeared to refer to illegal wiretaps in the 1970s - "a monumental invasion of privacy."

Lugar and fellow Republican John Chafee of Rhode Island say they are inclined to vote for Lake on the Intelligence Committee, which has 10 Republicans and nine Democrats. This means that if all the Democrats back Lake, the committee is likely to recommend his confirmation by the full Senate.
